name: Law Enforcement Directive
impact_assessment: SEC(2012) 72 (executive summary SEC(2012) 73), shared with GDPR
evidence_rating: thin: transposition and complaint statistics only; no independent or causal evidence on protection outcomes or law-enforcement effectiveness found
summary: The Law Enforcement Directive, which sets data protection rules for police and criminal courts, came with no monitoring indicators. The Commission's 2022 review found two-thirds of countries implemented it late and with gaps, and that complaints are rising; Member States say it improved awareness but some duties are burdensome. No study measures whether it actually changed how police handle personal data; a second Commission review is due in 2026.

indicators.objective: The 2012 LED proposal (COM(2012) 10) has no financial-statement indicators; monitoring relies on four-yearly Commission reports under Article 62 (first 2022, second due 2026)
Harmonised, high level of protection in policing and criminal justice
indicators.indicator: Transposition and conformity of national laws
indicators.evidence: Two-thirds of Member States missed the deadline; infringement cases against 19 Member States (2018), later one against Germany (2022). Transposition complete by 2019-2022 but gaps on storage limits, legal basis and supervisory powers.

More than a third of supervisory authorities reported more complaints; most inadmissible, some led to erasure/rectification orders; representative complaints rarely used. Council (2025) finds DPOs improved awareness but access requests and DPIAs burdensome.

indicators.objective: Facilitate exchange of data between law-enforcement authorities
indicators.evidence: Not measured; Council reports international transfer rules (Art. 37) hard to use in practice.

literature.citation: European Commission (2012), Impact Assessment for the data protection reform package (GDPR and Law Enforcement Directive), executive summary, SEC(2012) 73 (full IA SEC(2012) 72)
literature.title: Impact Assessment for the data protection reform package (GDPR and Law Enforcement Directive), executive summary
literature.outcomes: legal certainty; protection of individuals; police cooperation
literature.headline: Shared IA with the GDPR; for policing it identified fragmented rules under the 2008 Framework Decision and legal uncertainty for individuals and authorities; no quantified forecast for the LED
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's joint impact assessment argued that a single directive would end patchy data protection rules for police and courts, but gave no figures for this part.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), First report on application and functioning of the Data Protection Law Enforcement Directive (EU) 2016/680, COM(2022) 364
literature.title: First report on application and functioning of the Data Protection Law Enforcement Directive (EU) 2016/680
literature.method: transposition analysis, Member State and supervisory authority input, external study
literature.headline: Two-thirds of Member States late; 19 infringement procedures; transposition satisfactory overall with gaps; complaints rising; limited experience to judge effects
literature.summary_plain: The first review found most countries implemented the rules late and with gaps, and it was too early to judge their real effect.

literature.citation: Council of the European Union (2025), Council position and findings on the evaluation and review of the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), Council document ST 15616/25
literature.title: Council position and findings on the evaluation and review of the Law Enforcement Directive (LED)
literature.method: Member State observations (input to 2026 Commission review)
literature.headline: Harmonised framework welcomed; DPOs improved awareness and compliance; DPIAs, broad access requests and international-transfer rules perceived as burdensome
literature.summary_plain: Member States say the directive brought consistent rules and better data-protection awareness in police forces, but some obligations are burdensome in practice.
literature.interested_party: Member State governments (whose police and justice authorities are the regulated parties)
